Test both on your targets before committing large budgets.

blocks.text: FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData sells proxies the way prepaid phone plans sell minutes: one flat $1/GB balance that works across residential, mobile and datacenter pools. Static residential IPs start at $1.79 each in monthly bundles (20 for $49) with unlimited bandwidth. It is one of the cheapest ways into residential traffic, but it is a newer brand with less independent benchmarking than the established names.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte is a US proxy company that started life as Blazing SEO and built its name on dedicated datacenter proxies. Residential proxies have since become its main product. It sells them pay-as-you-go in four volume bands with traffic that never expires, sources at least part of its residential pool in-house, and offers country, region and city targeting. The notable limit is protocol support: its residential gateway does not support SOCKS5 or UDP.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Pricing: FloppyData vs Rayobyte

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP.
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $10 with FloppyData and $35 with Rayobyte: a 71% saving in FloppyData's favour. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $100 with FloppyData and $200 with Rayobyte: a 50% saving in FloppyData's favour. Look past the per-GB figure too. Rayobyte lets unused traffic carry forward, while FloppyData's allowance does not (check current terms). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

FloppyData and Rayobyte do not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. FloppyData lists '65M+ claimed (disputed)' and Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, FloppyData lists 148 (residential) countries and Rayobyte lists Global. On targeting, FloppyData offers country and city, while Rayobyte offers country, region and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. FloppyData supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in FloppyData's favour. On sessions, FloppyData offers rotating or sticky sessions, and Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Rayobyte wins. The deciding factor for Rayobyte: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires. The limitation on the FloppyData side: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.

SERP and rank tracking: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With FloppyData: workable for light tasks. With Rayobyte: usable, with no dedicated SERP product. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Social media and multi-account management: FloppyData wins. The deciding factor for FloppyData: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Rayobyte wins. The deciding factor for Rayobyte: city targeting and low prices at volume. The limitation on the FloppyData side: city targeting at a flat rate.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Rayobyte. Rayobyte has the edge here. Why: fewer carrier or ASN controls. How FloppyData compares: limited targeting depth and published data.
Tight budgets: FloppyData wins. The deciding factor for FloppyData: a flat $1/GB on any volume. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. FloppyData: No free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Verification and payment rules differ too. FloppyData: Light. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test FloppyData and Rayobyte before you commit
The quickest way to choose between FloppyData and Rayobyte is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (FloppyData: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations; Rayobyte: check current offer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, FloppyData comes out ahead in 2, Rayobyte in 3, and 1 is a tie. That makes Rayobyte the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments, while Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
